title: five infuriating energy transition fumbles 2026 07 30
author: Gavin Maguire
text:
LITTLETON, Colorado, July 31 (Reuters) - The good news about the global energy transition is that most of the key technologies now work.
Solar panels work. Wind turbines work. Batteries work. Electric buses work. Hydrogen electrolysers generally work too.
The bad news is that governments, utilities and companies around the world keep finding creative new ways to stop those technologies from actually delivering what they're supposed to.
The transition's biggest obstacles are no longer scientific. Increasingly, they are administrative, logistical and political.
Put simply, humanity appears to have spent ​years perfecting the shiny green hardware while neglecting the boring supporting infrastructure.
The result is a growing catalogue of costly own goals.
Here are five of the most infuriating.
Ireland may have produced the defining ‌image of the modern energy transition: rows of brand-new electric buses sitting in storage yards because there are not enough charging facilities ready to put them into service.
More than 130 battery-electric buses were manufactured and delivered more than two years ago, but charging infrastructure at depots lagged behind, forcing authorities to continue running diesel buses while the electric fleet sits idle.
On top of the estimated €500,000 spent on each bus, millions more has been spent on storage and maintenance of scores of the still-unused green buses while the problem is being addressed.
The difficult part was supposed to be developing and purchasing the buses.
Installing chargers should have been comparatively ​straightforward.
Instead, planners managed to acquire the vehicles before ensuring there was a way to charge them.
Infrastructure first, procurement second.
The energy transition increasingly hinges not on breakthrough technologies but on getting the sequencing right.
If Ireland's buses represent a ​local planning failure, India demonstrates the problem at truly industrial scale.
India has become one of the world's fastest-growing renewable energy markets. But transmission construction has struggled to keep pace.
Industry groups have warned that more than ⁠50 gigawatts of renewable projects have become stranded by a combination of transmission delays, regulatory bottlenecks and missing power supply agreements.
Reuters reported that unfinished transmission infrastructure in major renewable hubs such as Rajasthan and Gujarat has delayed project commissioning.
The numbers are staggering. Fifty gigawatts is roughly equivalent ​to the generating capacity of an entire midsized industrialised economy, and represents around one-fifth of the total installed capacity of renewable electricity supply in the country.
The world spent two decades worrying about whether solar panels were affordable enough.
Now that they are, the constraint turns out ​to be transmission lines, permits and paperwork.
The solar farms arrived on schedule. The wires did not.
Every renewable energy story eventually becomes a transmission story.
Electricity may travel at close to the speed of light, but new power lines move at the speed of local permitting processes.
Few countries embraced electrification as enthusiastically as the Netherlands.
The Dutch promoted electric vehicles, heat pumps and cleaner industrial processes at remarkable speed. Unfortunately, demand for electricity expanded faster than the grid itself.
The result has been severe congestion
, opens new tab
 across parts of the network, with businesses and housing developments increasingly finding themselves on waiting lists for electricity connections.
Several projects have reportedly faced delays ​because the grid lacks sufficient spare capacity.
This wasn't a failure caused by climate sceptics, fossil fuel lobbying or technological shortcomings. It was caused by success.
The country became so effective at encouraging electrification that the underlying network struggled to keep up.
The Dutch solved the demand side ​of the energy transition before solving the extension cord.
Electricity grids are not optional extras. They are the foundation upon which every other decarbonisation strategy rests.
No clean-energy concept has received more hype over the past five years than green hydrogen.
Which makes Australia's Whyalla project such a cautionary ‌tale.
South Australia established ⁠a dedicated Office of Hydrogen Power and committed nearly A$600 million ($421 million) toward a flagship hydrogen project centred on Whyalla.
The project was promoted as a groundbreaking demonstration of hydrogen's role in power generation and industrial decarbonisation.
But the venture ultimately unravelled amid cost pressures, market headwinds and the crisis surrounding the Whyalla steelworks.
The project was shelved, the hydrogen office dissolved, and auditors later reported hundreds of millions of dollars in spending, including substantial asset write-downs linked to preliminary project work.
This was not merely a delayed project. It was a reminder that enthusiasm and economics are not the same thing.
Hydrogen became the energy transition's favourite conference presentation, but PowerPoint slides have a poor record of generating commercial returns.
Pilot projects are necessary.
Expensive bets placed before markets, customers and economics are fully established are considerably riskier.
California offers an unusual example of failure ​through success.
For years the state pushed aggressively to expand solar generation. ​It succeeded.
So successfully, in fact, that the grid increasingly struggles to ⁠absorb all the electricity produced during certain periods.
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, California curtailed around 3 terawatt hours (TWh) of wind and solar generation in each of the past two years, which is as much electricity as roughly 500,000 homes use annually in the state.
Solar accounted for the vast majority of those reductions. Oversupply, congestion and operational constraints have also contributed to increasingly frequent periods of negative power prices.
California worked hard to solve one problem: too little solar generation.
It now finds itself grappling with a different problem: too much solar generation at the wrong times.
There is something uniquely maddening about ​building clean electricity facilities only to switch ⁠them off because the grid cannot fully use what they produce.
Installing renewable generation is only half the challenge.
Storage, transmission and flexible electricity demand are becoming equally important.
These five examples span three continents and involve different technologies, governments and market structures.
Yet they all share the same underlying flaw.
The equipment works. The planning does not.
Again and again, policymakers have focused on the visible symbols of the transition — buses, solar farms, hydrogen plants and electric vehicles — while overlooking the less glamorous systems that make those assets useful.
Every electric bus requires a charger.
Every wind farm requires a transmission line.
Every hydrogen project ⁠requires a customer.
Every energy ​transition requires an electrical grid capable of supporting it.
The encouraging news is that these mistakes are largely fixable.
The worrying news is that the same lesson keeps being ​learned over and over again: in energy, the boring stuff matters most.
And while nobody ever built a multi-trillion-dollar industrial revolution without making some costly mistakes, it would be nice if the next generation of green fumbles involved fewer own goals.
